options: an executive presidential system to Nigeria
questions.explanation: Nigeria abandoned the British parliamentary model in favor of an American-style executive presidential system.

questions.text: The primary duty of the civil service in a state is to
options: contest elections and form political parties
implement and execute government policies continuously
adjudicate civil and criminal cases in court
questions.explanation: Career civil servants provide professional administrative execution of state policies across changing political regimes.

questions.text: The main objective of pressure groups in a democratic society is to
options: capture state executive power through elections
influence government policies in favor of its members' interests
replace the legislature in passing national budgets
organize military coups against civil administrations
questions.explanation: Pressure groups lobby policymakers to secure specific economic, social, or professional goals without running candidates for public office.

questions.text: Political parties differ from pressure groups because political parties
options: sponsor candidates to win elections and form government
refuse to participate in any electoral process
questions.explanation: Parties sponsor candidates in elections specifically to capture state power and form the government.

questions.text: Electoral malpractice includes illegal activities such as
options: vote-buying, ballot box snatching, and falsification of results
questions.explanation: Vote buying, ballot box snatching, and falsification of results undermine free and fair elections.

questions.text: The independent body responsible for conducting federal elections in Nigeria is the
questions.explanation: The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) registers voters, delineates constituencies, and organizes polls.

questions.text: The process by which citizens acquire political values, beliefs, and orientations is called
questions.explanation: Family, schools, peers, and media act as key agents of political socialization throughout a person's life.

questions.text: Public opinion is best defined as
options: the collective views and attitudes of a population regarding public issues
the official position of the government on foreign policy
the rulings of the supreme court
the manifesto of the ruling political party
questions.explanation: It represents the collective views, attitudes, and beliefs held by a population regarding public policies and leaders.

questions.text: The term "gerrymandering" refers to the practice of
options: manipulating electoral boundaries to favor a particular party or candidate
questions.explanation: Manipulating electoral boundaries for partisan advantage distorts fair representation.

questions.text: The foundational legal framework that guarantees fundamental human rights in Nigeria is the
questions.explanation: Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution entrenches civil liberties and human rights protections.

questions.text: The international organization established in 1945 to maintain global peace and security is the
questions.explanation: The United Nations succeeded the League of Nations to foster international cooperation and security.

questions.text: The administrative headquarters of the African Union (AU) is located in
questions.explanation: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, hosts the primary assembly summits and headquarters of the AU Commission.

questions.text: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was founded through the Treaty of Lagos in
questions.explanation: The treaty was signed on May 28, 1975, to promote regional economic integration.

questions.text: The Commonwealth of Nations is an association comprising mainly
options: former territories of the British Empire
questions.explanation: Former territories of the British Empire maintain voluntary cooperation and shared democratic values through the Commonwealth.

questions.text: The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) was established to
options: provide welfare payments to poor countries
coordinate petroleum policies and stabilize international oil markets
questions.explanation: OPEC coordinates petroleum policies and production quotas among member states to stabilize international oil markets.

questions.text: The principle of non-alignment during the Cold War meant that a state
options: remained independent and did not join either the Western or Eastern military blocs
aligned fully with the United States
questions.explanation: Non-aligned nations maintained independent foreign policies, refusing to join formal military pacts with either the Western or Eastern blocs.

questions.text: The primary objective of Nigeria's foreign policy has traditionally been the
options: protection of national interest, African unity, and economic well-being
establishment of military dominance in West Africa
promotion of dictatorship in neighboring states
questions.explanation: Safeguarding national interest, African unity, and the economic well-being of citizens guides Nigerian diplomacy.

questions.text: The judicial organ of government checks the other branches through the power of
questions.explanation: Judicial review enables courts to nullify unconstitutional legislative acts or executive actions.

questions.text: The concept of rule of law implies that
options: the president is above the law
no one is above the law, and all are subject to it
questions.explanation: No individual—regardless of political office or wealth—stands above the law of the land.

questions.text: Good governance is fundamentally measured by indicators such as
options: transparency, accountability, rule of law, and responsiveness
questions.explanation: Transparency, accountability, rule of law, responsiveness, and equity define successful governance structures.

questions.text: The concept of 'judicial activism' in constitutional interpretation refers to
options: judges strictly applying the literal text of the constitution
judges interpreting the constitution broadly to address contemporary social issues
judges refusing to hear constitutional cases
judges deferring entirely to executive branch decisions
questions.explanation: Judicial activism involves judges interpreting constitutional provisions in light of modern societal needs, sometimes going beyond the literal text to protect rights and address injustices.

questions.text: A 'proportional representation' electoral system is designed to
options: ensure the candidate with the most votes wins the constituency seat
allocate legislative seats to parties based on the percentage of votes they receive
eliminate the need for political parties in elections
restrict voting rights to property owners only
questions.explanation: Proportional representation ensures that the number of parliamentary seats a party wins is directly proportional to the total votes it receives nationwide.

questions.text: The principle of 'subsidiarity' in federal governance implies that
options: all decisions must be made by the central government
decisions should be made at the lowest competent level of government closest to citizens
sub-national governments have no authority over local affairs
the judiciary must approve all government decisions
questions.explanation: Subsidiarity ensures that governance decisions are taken at the level closest to the affected citizens, promoting local autonomy and democratic participation.

questions.text: A 'constitutional monarchy' differs from an 'absolute monarchy' because in a constitutional monarchy
options: the monarch holds unlimited legislative and executive powers
the monarch's powers are defined and limited by a written or unwritten constitution
the monarch is elected by popular vote every five years
questions.explanation: Constitutional monarchies restrict royal authority through constitutional provisions, with real governance powers typically exercised by an elected parliament and prime minister.

questions.text: The 'lame duck' period in presidential systems refers to the time
options: when a president is newly elected and awaiting inauguration
after an election when the outgoing president has reduced influence before the successor takes office
when the legislature overrides the presidential veto
when the judiciary declares presidential actions unconstitutional
questions.explanation: A lame duck president is one who is in office between the election of their successor and the inauguration, often having diminished political influence.

questions.text: The legal doctrine of 'stare decisis' obliges courts to
options: follow established precedents in deciding similar cases
amend the constitution through judicial rulings
refer all constitutional cases to the executive
questions.explanation: Stare decisis (Latin for 'to stand by things decided') requires courts to uphold previous rulings to ensure consistency, predictability, and stability in law.

questions.text: A 'unicameral legislature' is characterized by
options: an upper and lower house of parliament
legislative powers vested in the executive
questions.explanation: A unicameral legislature has only one chamber or house, as opposed to bicameral legislatures with two chambers.

questions.text: The 'entrenchment clause' in a constitution refers to provisions
options: that can be amended through ordinary legislative processes
that are protected from ordinary amendment and require special procedures to change
that grant absolute powers to the executive
that abolishes the judicial branch of government
questions.explanation: Entrenched clauses are fundamental constitutional provisions that require special, difficult amendment procedures to protect them from arbitrary changes.

questions.text: A 'referendum' is a direct democratic device that allows citizens to
options: vote directly on a specific legislative proposal or constitutional amendment
questions.explanation: Referendums place specific policy or constitutional questions directly before the electorate for approval or rejection, bypassing legislative processes.

questions.text: The 'Westminster model' of parliamentary government is characterized by
options: a strict separation of executive and legislative powers
the fusion of executive and legislative branches with the executive drawn from parliament
an executive president elected independently of the legislature
absolute dominance of the judiciary over other branches
questions.explanation: The Westminster model features a parliamentary system where the prime minister and cabinet are members of parliament, accountable to the legislature through collective responsibility.

questions.text: A 'pocket veto' occurs when
options: the legislature overrides the president's veto
the president takes no action on a bill and congress adjourns before the bill becomes law
the judiciary declares a law unconstitutional
the executive returns a bill to parliament with recommended amendments
questions.explanation: A pocket veto happens when the executive does not sign a bill within the constitutional timeframe and the legislature has adjourned, preventing a regular veto override.

questions.text: The concept of 'nation-building' primarily involves
options: fostering a shared national identity, unity, and social cohesion among diverse groups
expanding territorial boundaries through military conquest
questions.explanation: Nation-building encompasses efforts to create a unified national identity and social cohesion among citizens, particularly in culturally and ethnically diverse states.

questions.text: A 'writ of habeas corpus' is a legal instrument that protects citizens against
options: arbitrary detention without trial or legal justification
questions.explanation: Habeas corpus requires authorities to produce a detained person before a court and justify their detention, protecting against unlawful imprisonment.

questions.text: The political concept of 'neo-colonialism' refers to
options: the direct military occupation of former colonies
the continued economic, political, and cultural influence of former colonial powers over independent states
the complete independence and self-sufficiency of former colonies
the establishment of new colonial territories
questions.explanation: Neo-colonialism describes the indirect control exercised by former colonial powers over newly independent states through economic dependency, cultural influence, and political interference.

questions.text: An 'interpellation' in parliamentary procedure involves
options: a formal judicial review of legislation
a formal parliamentary question to a government minister requiring an answer
the election of a new parliamentary speaker
questions.explanation: Interpellation is a parliamentary mechanism where legislators formally question government ministers about their policies and actions, ensuring executive accountability.

questions.text: The 'harmonious construction' principle in constitutional interpretation requires courts to
options: interpret constitutional provisions in isolation from each other
interpret different provisions of the constitution consistently with each other
defer to the executive branch for constitutional interpretation
questions.explanation: Harmonious construction requires that all constitutional provisions be interpreted as mutually consistent, avoiding contradictions and giving meaning to every clause.

questions.text: The 'spoils system' in public administration refers to
options: the practice of rewarding political supporters with government appointments
questions.explanation: The spoils system involves distributing public offices and rewards to political loyalists and supporters, often at the expense of competence and merit.

questions.text: A 'constituent assembly' is a body convened specifically to
options: draft, debate, and adopt a new constitution or constitutional amendments
questions.explanation: Constituent assemblies are constitutional conventions established specifically for the purpose of drafting or revising the fundamental law of a state.

questions.text: The 'due process' clause in constitutional law requires that
options: all government actions must be secret
government must respect all legal rights owed to citizens, including fair procedures
citizens must obey all laws without question
the legislature can override judicial decisions
questions.explanation: Due process requires that the government respect established legal rights and follow fair procedures before depriving citizens of life, liberty, or property.

questions.text: The concept of 'fiscal federalism' deals primarily with
options: the allocation of revenue sources and expenditure responsibilities among levels of government
the complete centralization of all government revenues
the elimination of state and local governments
the privatization of all public services
questions.explanation: Fiscal federalism examines how revenues are raised and expenditures are allocated across federal, state, and local governments in a federal system.

questions.text: A 'minority government' is formed when
options: a party holds an absolute majority of parliamentary seats
the governing party has fewer than half the seats and must rely on other parties for legislative support
questions.explanation: A minority government occurs when the ruling party does not have an absolute parliamentary majority, requiring support from opposition parties to pass legislation.

questions.text: The 'principle of legality' in administrative law requires that
options: government decisions must be politically popular
government decisions and actions must be authorized by law
all laws must be approved by the executive
questions.explanation: The principle of legality mandates that all government actions must have a clear legal basis and be consistent with existing legal frameworks.

questions.text: A 'plebiscite' is a direct vote by eligible citizens on
options: a specific issue of national importance or constitutional change
selecting a new head of government
questions.explanation: A plebiscite is a direct vote on a specific political issue or constitutional matter, similar to a referendum but often used for broader national questions.

questions.text: The 'principle of legality' in criminal justice establishes that
options: all accused persons are presumed guilty until proven innocent
no act can be punished as a crime unless it was specifically prohibited by law
judges can create new crimes through court rulings
questions.explanation: The principle of legality (nullum crimen sine lege) ensures that no one can be convicted of a crime that was not legally defined and punished at the time it was committed.

questions.text: The 'merit system' in public administration is characterized by
options: appointments and promotions based on political connections
appointments and promotions based on qualifications, competence, and performance
questions.explanation: The merit system ensures that civil service appointments and career advancement are determined by qualifications, competitive examinations, and demonstrated performance.

questions.text: A 'unitary state' differs from a 'federal state' because in a unitary state
options: the central government shares sovereignty with regional governments
all governmental powers are concentrated in the central government
there are multiple levels of independent judicial systems
questions.explanation: In a unitary state, the central government holds supreme authority, and any regional or local governments derive their powers from and are subject to the central authority.

questions.text: The 'office of profit' concept in constitutional law refers to
options: the ability of legislators to engage in private business
positions that would disqualify an individual from holding legislative office due to potential conflicts of interest
the requirement for all public officials to be wealthy
questions.explanation: The office of profit principle prevents legislators from holding certain other public offices to avoid conflicts between legislative duties and executive positions.

questions.text: The 'civilian control of the military' is a fundamental principle ensuring that
options: military commanders appoint civilian government officials
elected civilian authorities exercise ultimate authority over the armed forces
the constitution is suspended during emergencies
questions.explanation: Civilian control of the military ensures that democratically elected civilian leaders have ultimate authority over military institutions, preventing military intervention in politics.

questions.text: A 'residual power' in a federal constitution refers to
options: powers explicitly delegated to the federal government
powers not specifically assigned to any level of government, falling to the states
powers exclusively exercised by the federal government
powers completely abolished by the constitution
questions.explanation: Residual powers are those governmental authorities not specifically enumerated in the constitution and therefore retained by the federating units or states.

questions.text: The 'prerogative of mercy' is a constitutional power that allows the executive to
options: veto all legislation passed by parliament
pardon or grant leniency to convicted offenders
appoint all judges to the courts
questions.explanation: The prerogative of mercy allows the executive to pardon convicted offenders, reduce sentences, or grant clemency, functioning as a check on judicial power.

questions.text: A 'concurrent list' in a federal constitution contains powers
options: exercised exclusively by the federal government
exercised jointly by both federal and state governments
questions.explanation: Concurrent lists contain matters over which both the federal and state governments can legislate, with federal law typically prevailing in case of conflict.

questions.text: The 'popular initiative' is a direct democracy mechanism allowing citizens to
options: propose new legislation or constitutional amendments through petition
questions.explanation: Popular initiative empowers citizens to propose legislation or constitutional changes by gathering a sufficient number of signatures to force legislative consideration or a public vote.

questions.text: The 'leadership code' in many African constitutions aims to prevent
options: public corruption and abuse of office by public officials
questions.explanation: Leadership codes impose ethical standards, financial disclosure requirements, and restrictions on public officials to combat corruption and self-enrichment.

questions.text: The concept of 'distributive justice' in political philosophy concerns
options: fair allocation of resources, benefits, and burdens among members of society
strict equality of outcomes regardless of contribution
questions.explanation: Distributive justice examines how society's resources, rights, and duties should be fairly distributed among its members.

questions.text: A 'supranational organization' is one in which
options: member states delegate some sovereignty to a central authority that can make binding decisions
membership is entirely voluntary and non-binding
decisions require unanimous consent of all members
questions.explanation: Supranational organizations have authority that exceeds that of individual member states in certain areas, with decisions that can be binding on all members.

questions.text: The 'social contract theory' in political philosophy posits that
options: political authority originates from the collective consent of the governed
the state is a natural phenomenon without human creation
government exists primarily to protect private property
questions.explanation: Social contract theory suggests that individuals voluntarily surrender some freedoms to the state in exchange for protection and order, creating legitimate political authority.

questions.text: The 'public interest theory' of regulation holds that government regulation should primarily
options: serve the broad welfare and interests of the general public
advance the interests of government officials
questions.explanation: Public interest theory asserts that regulation should be designed to protect and advance the welfare of society as a whole, not just particular groups.

questions.text: A 'shadow cabinet' is a parliamentary institution in which
options: the ruling party's ministers hold informal meetings
opposition party members hold portfolios and scrutinize government ministers
questions.explanation: A shadow cabinet comprises opposition party members who monitor and critique government ministries, providing alternative policies and holding the government accountable.

questions.text: The 'justiciability' of a legal issue refers to whether
options: the issue is appropriate and suitable for judicial resolution
the legislature has considered the issue
questions.explanation: Justiciability determines whether a legal dispute can be properly heard and resolved by a court of law.

questions.text: A 'mandate' in electoral politics refers to
options: a legal requirement to vote in all elections
the authority granted to a political party by voters to implement its policies
the requirement for political parties to have constitutions
the minimum age for political candidates
questions.explanation: A mandate is the authority given by voters to a political party or candidate to implement their promised policies after winning an election.

questions.text: The 'national interest' concept in foreign policy refers to
options: the interests of the ruling political party
the fundamental values, security, and economic objectives of a state in international affairs
the personal interests of the head of state
questions.explanation: National interest comprises the core values and strategic objectives that guide a state's foreign policy decisions and international engagements.

questions.text: A 'professional politician' is someone who
options: makes politics their primary career, often holding public office regularly
questions.explanation: Professional politicians dedicate their primary career to politics, typically holding elective or appointed political offices as their main occupation.

questions.text: The 'liberal democratic' model emphasizes
options: collective ownership and limited individual freedoms
individual rights, representative democracy, free markets, and constitutional limits on power
absolute state control over all economic activities
questions.explanation: Liberal democracy combines democratic representation with protection of individual liberties and limited government through constitutional constraints.

questions.text: The 'bureaucratic model' of administration, as described by Max Weber, is characterized by
options: hierarchical authority, clear rules, specialization, and impersonality
elected officials as the primary administrators
questions.explanation: Weber's ideal bureaucracy features a hierarchy of authority, written rules, specialized roles, and impersonal relationships to ensure efficiency and consistency.

questions.text: A 'devolution' of powers involves
options: concentrating all powers in the central government
the statutory transfer of certain governmental powers from central to regional or local governments
merging all levels of government into a single unit
questions.explanation: Devolution involves the legal transfer of specific governmental powers and responsibilities from central authorities to regional or local governments through legislation.

questions.text: The 'consociational democracy' model is designed to accommodate
options: deeply divided societies through power-sharing, group autonomy, and proportional representation
complete assimilation of all minority groups
absolute dominance of the largest ethnic group
questions.explanation: Consociational democracy manages divided societies through mechanisms like power-sharing, group representation, and mutual vetoes to prevent inter-group conflict.

questions.text: The 'separation of judiciary' principle ensures that
options: judges are appointed by the executive
the judicial branch is institutionally independent from the executive and legislative branches
courts must always follow executive directions
judges serve only at the pleasure of the legislature
questions.explanation: Judicial independence requires that courts be structurally and institutionally separate from the other branches, ensuring impartial and independent adjudication.

questions.text: A 'state of exception' in constitutional law refers to
options: the complete absence of all government authority
the temporary suspension of normal constitutional rights and procedures during emergencies
the permanent abolition of constitutional government
the removal of all executive powers
questions.explanation: A state of exception permits temporary derogation from normal constitutional rules and rights in response to extraordinary threats to the state.

questions.text: The 'eminent domain' power allows the state to
options: appropriate private property for public use upon payment of just compensation
questions.explanation: Eminent domain is the sovereign power to take private property for public purposes, subject to constitutional requirements of just compensation.

questions.text: The 'lobbying' process in democratic systems involves
options: attempting to influence government decisions through legitimate advocacy, persuasion, and information provision
questions.explanation: Lobbying is the legitimate advocacy by interest groups to influence policy decisions and legislation through communication and persuasion.

questions.text: The 'doctrine of necessity' in constitutional jurisprudence justifies what type of government action?
options: Actions that strictly follow all constitutional provisions
Extra-constitutional actions essential to preserve state existence during exceptional crises
Actions that permanently suspend the constitution
Actions taken only with legislative approval
questions.explanation: The doctrine of necessity provides justification for actions that may technically violate constitutional provisions when such actions are essential to preserve the state's continuity and stability.

questions.text: What does 'horizontal application' of fundamental rights mean in constitutional law?
options: Rights only apply to relationships between state and citizens
Constitutional rights can be enforced between private individuals or entities
Rights are only applicable to federal government actions
questions.explanation: Horizontal application allows constitutional rights to be invoked in disputes between private parties, extending protection beyond just state-citizen relationships.

questions.text: What is the primary function of 'legislative oversight' in parliamentary democracy?
options: Parliament making laws without executive input
Monitoring and supervising executive branch activities
questions.explanation: Legislative oversight enables parliaments to scrutinize executive actions, ensuring accountability, transparency, and proper implementation of laws.

questions.text: A 'quasi-federal' system of government exhibits which characteristics?
options: Both parliamentary and presidential system features
Federal and unitary system features with significant centralization but some regional autonomy
questions.explanation: Quasi-federal systems blend federal and unitary features, with significant central authority while granting limited autonomy to regional governments.

questions.text: What does the 'concurrent majority' principle require in political decision-making?
options: A simple majority of voters to approve all legislation
Major decisions require approval from various distinct interests or groups
questions.explanation: Concurrent majority requires that significant decisions receive support from multiple distinct societal groups, protecting minority interests against majority tyranny.

questions.text: What does 'natural law' jurisprudence posit about legal systems?
options: All laws must be created by legislatures
A universal moral order exists that human laws derive legitimacy from
Laws are purely products of social convention
The state has unlimited authority to define law
questions.explanation: Natural law theory holds that certain universal moral principles exist independently of human-made law, and positive laws derive their legitimacy from conformity with these principles.

questions.text: What does the concept of 'political legitimacy' refer to in governance?
options: The legal requirement for periodic elections
General acceptance of a government's right to rule by its citizens
The financial resources available to a government
The military strength of a government
questions.explanation: Political legitimacy exists when citizens accept a government's authority to rule based on consent, legality, performance, or traditional recognition.

questions.text: What does 'parliamentary privilege' protect for legislators?
options: Absolute immunity from all criminal prosecution
Freedom of speech and conduct of parliamentary business without external interference
questions.explanation: Parliamentary privileges protect legislators' freedom of speech in parliamentary proceedings and provide immunity from certain legal actions while performing legislative duties.

questions.text: What does the 'imperial presidency' concept describe?
options: The legislature dominating all executive functions
Executive accumulating excessive power and dominance over other branches
Power being entirely decentralized to local governments
questions.explanation: The imperial presidency occurs when executive power expands significantly, often surpassing constitutional limits and dominating other branches of government.

questions.text: What does 'civil society' encompass in political theory?
options: Voluntary associations, NGOs, and social movements operating independently of the state
The military establishment and security apparatus
questions.explanation: Civil society comprises the diverse range of non-governmental organizations and voluntary associations that exist between the state and individual citizens.

questions.text: What does 'judicial self-restraint' encourage judges to do?
options: Actively rewrite laws to align with contemporary values
Defer to other branches and avoid striking down laws unless clearly unconstitutional
Substitute their policy preferences for legislative decisions
questions.explanation: Judicial self-restraint urges courts to exercise caution in invalidating legislation, deferring to the legislature's judgment when constitutional questions are debatable.

questions.text: What characterizes a 'mixed constitution' in political theory?
options: Multiple forms of government combined, such as monarchic, aristocratic, and democratic elements
questions.explanation: Mixed constitutions combine different governmental forms to balance competing interests and prevent any single element from dominating.

questions.text: What is the 'agent-principal problem' in democratic theory?
options: The legal relationship between lawyers and clients
Elected officials pursuing personal interests rather than constituents' interests
The relationship between employers and employees
The authority of principals over schools
questions.explanation: The agent-principal problem arises when representatives pursue their own interests rather than faithfully serving the interests of citizens who elected them.

questions.text: What does the 'principle of tolerance' require in democratic societies?
options: Citizens to support all government policies unconditionally
Acceptance and respect for diverse views, beliefs, and practices despite disagreements
questions.explanation: Tolerance in democratic societies requires respecting the rights of others to hold and express beliefs different from one's own, even when strongly disagreed with.

questions.text: What is a 'specialized agency' of the United Nations?
options: A military command under UN authority
An autonomous international organization working with the UN on specific functional areas
A regional political bloc within the UN
The UN Security Council's enforcement mechanism
questions.explanation: Specialized UN agencies like WHO, ILO, and UNESCO are autonomous international organizations with specific mandates, cooperating with the UN through special agreements.

questions.text: What does 'veto player' theory describe in political science?
options: Only the UN Security Council veto power
Individuals or groups whose agreement is necessary for policy change
Legislators who always vote against government proposals
The judiciary's power to strike down legislation
questions.explanation: Veto player analysis identifies actors whose consent is required for policy change, affecting the stability and pace of political reform.

questions.text: What does 'rational choice' theory assume about political actors?
options: All political actors act purely irrationally
Individuals make decisions based on self-interest and utility maximization
Political behavior is purely determined by social class
Voters never consider their own interests
questions.explanation: Rational choice theory models political behavior as individuals making calculated decisions to maximize personal benefits, often in an analytical framework.

questions.text: What does the 'path dependency' concept explain in political development?
options: Political parties always selecting new leaders
Historical decisions constraining future policy options
All political systems inevitably moving toward democracy
questions.explanation: Path dependency suggests that past decisions shape and constrain future choices, making certain outcomes more likely while foreclosing others.

questions.text: What does 'principal-agent relationship' involve in constitutional governance?
options: Judiciary acting as principal over the legislature
Citizens as principals delegating authority to representatives as agents
The executive dominating all government functions
questions.explanation: Principal-agent relationships in governance occur when citizens delegate authority to representatives who are expected to act on their behalf.

questions.text: What does 'deliberative democracy' emphasize in political decision-making?
options: Reasoned discussion, reflection, and reasoned argument
questions.explanation: Deliberative democracy prioritizes inclusive, reasoned discourse where citizens discuss and debate issues to reach consensus-based decisions.

questions.text: What does 'overlapping consensus' refer to in political philosophy?
options: Agreement among citizens that all laws are unjust
Different groups supporting the same political principles for different reasons
Complete rejection of all political institutions
questions.explanation: Overlapping consensus occurs when diverse groups with different comprehensive doctrines nevertheless converge on the same fundamental political principles.

questions.text: What does the 'institutionalism' approach emphasize in political science?
options: The role of formal and informal institutions in shaping political behavior
The analysis of public opinion polls only
questions.explanation: Institutionalism studies how formal rules, organizations, and informal norms structure political interactions and influence policy outcomes.

questions.text: What does 'public choice' school apply economic analysis to?
options: Political decision-making, voting, bureaucracy, and collective action
questions.explanation: Public choice theory uses economic tools to analyze political behavior, including politicians' self-interest, bureaucratic growth, and the nature of collective decision-making.

questions.text: What is a 'catch-all party' in political party systems?
options: A party representing only a specific social class
A party seeking to attract voters across different social groups by reducing ideological rigidity
A party refusing to participate in national elections
A party focusing exclusively on a single policy issue
questions.explanation: Catch-all parties broaden their appeal across diverse social groups by adopting flexible ideological positions and inclusive policy platforms.

questions.text: What does 'clientelism' or 'patronage' involve in political practice?
options: Distribution of resources and benefits in exchange for political support
questions.explanation: Clientelism involves politicians providing material benefits or services to supporters in exchange for electoral support, often undermining meritocratic governance.

questions.text: What does 'state capacity' refer to in political science?
options: The physical size of a country's territory
A state's ability to implement policies, maintain order, and effectively govern
The total economic output of a nation
questions.explanation: State capacity measures a government's effectiveness in implementing policies, delivering services, and maintaining control over its territory.

questions.text: What does 'rent-seeking' behavior describe in political economy?
options: Individuals paying market rates for housing
Obtaining economic benefits through political manipulation rather than productive activity
questions.explanation: Rent-seeking occurs when individuals or groups influence political decisions to gain economic benefits without creating corresponding value, often at society's expense.

questions.text: What does the 'principle of accountability' require in democratic governance?
options: Government to operate in complete secrecy
Public officials to be answerable for their actions to the citizenry
Complete autonomy of all government agencies
Civil servants to have no oversight
questions.explanation: Accountability requires that government officials answer for their conduct and decisions, with mechanisms allowing citizens to sanction or reward political behavior.

questions.text: What does the 'responsiveness' principle require of government institutions?
options: Adapting to citizens' needs and expressed preferences
Executives maintaining their own policy preferences regardless of public views
questions.explanation: Responsive governments adjust policies and decisions based on citizen preferences and emerging needs, maintaining a democratic feedback loop.

questions.text: What do 'distributive policies' of government primarily concern?
options: Allocation of public resources, benefits, and services to various segments of society
Operation of the criminal justice system
questions.explanation: Distributive policies determine how government resources are allocated among different social groups, regions, or programs, affecting social welfare and equity.

questions.text: What does the 'regulatory state' concept describe?
options: State activities focusing primarily on regulation and rule-setting rather than direct production
Regulation entirely left to the private sector
questions.explanation: The regulatory state emphasizes government's role in setting and enforcing rules governing economic and social activities rather than direct service provision.

questions.text: What characterizes the 'developmental state' model?
options: Minimal government intervention in the economy
Strong state-led economic planning and intervention for rapid industrial development
Government operating only as a night-watchman
questions.explanation: Developmental states feature active government involvement in directing economic growth through strategic industrial policy, subsidies, and state enterprises.

questions.text: What does the 'failed state' concept describe?
options: A state with extremely high economic growth rates
A state that cannot perform basic functions like maintaining order, delivering services, or enforcing laws
A state operating with complete efficiency
A state that has never experienced political conflict
questions.explanation: Failed states lose control over territory, fail to provide basic services, and can no longer maintain legitimate authority or effective governance.

questions.text: What is a 'hybrid regime' in political classification?
options: A purely democratic system with no authoritarian features
A system combining democracy and authoritarianism with elections lacking full democratic substance
A system with no governmental institutions
questions.explanation: Hybrid regimes include formal democratic institutions like elections but exhibit significant authoritarian features that limit meaningful political competition.

questions.text: What does 'competitive authoritarianism' describe?
options: Regimes that allow no elections whatsoever
Regimes that hold elections competitive enough to require minimal fairness but not enough to threaten regime control
questions.explanation: Competitive authoritarian regimes maintain the formal trappings of democracy while manipulating elections and institutions to ensure regime victory.

questions.text: What is a 'strong state' in political science?
options: A state with military controlling the government
A state with capacity to effectively implement policies and maintain order across its territory
A state with overwhelming economic resources compared to citizens
A state with a highly centralized political system
questions.explanation: A strong state has the institutional capability to enforce laws, collect taxes, implement policies, and maintain control throughout its territory.

questions.text: What does the 'weak state' concept describe?
options: A state with no international recognition
A state lacking institutional capacity to effectively implement policies or maintain control
A state with a very small population
A state operating with a limited economic budget
questions.explanation: Weak states struggle to enforce laws, provide services, or maintain authority throughout their territory due to limited institutional capacity.

questions.text: What does the 'administrative state' emphasize?
options: Bureaucratic administration and implementation of public policies
questions.explanation: The administrative state focuses on the extensive bureaucracy and regulatory apparatus that implements policies and manages public affairs.

questions.text: What is a 'natural monopoly' in economic regulation?
options: Industries where competition is impossible and a single provider is most efficient
Industries where multiple firms compete effectively
Industries where government has no regulatory authority
Industries where entry is completely open to all businesses
questions.explanation: Natural monopolies occur when the most efficient market structure involves a single provider due to significant economies of scale or infrastructure costs.

questions.text: What does 'global governance' describe in international relations?
options: The rule of a single world government
Cooperative arrangements and institutions for managing transnational issues across sovereign states
The complete absence of international cooperation
questions.explanation: Global governance encompasses the diverse international institutions, treaties, and cooperative mechanisms established to address issues transcending national borders.

questions.text: What is an 'epistemic community' in international relations?
options: Networks of professionals and experts sharing knowledge and influencing policy formation
questions.explanation: Epistemic communities consist of experts from various fields who share beliefs and work to influence policy through specialized knowledge and professional networks.

questions.text: What does 'soft power' describe in international relations?
questions.explanation: Soft power relies on cultural appeal, positive values, and attractive policies to persuade other states to adopt desired positions without coercion.

questions.text: What does 'hard power' refer to in international relations?
options: The cultural attractiveness of a nation
Military and economic might used to compel or coerce other states
The moral authority of a country
questions.explanation: Hard power involves the use of military force, economic sanctions, and other forms of coercion to achieve foreign policy objectives.

questions.text: What is 'diplomatic recognition' in international law?
options: Formal acknowledgment by one state of another state's existence and political status
questions.explanation: Diplomatic recognition is a political act where one state formally acknowledges another's sovereignty and international legal personality.

questions.text: What are 'jus cogens' norms in international law?
options: Treaty provisions that are easily amended
Peremptory norms from which no derogation is permitted, such as prohibitions against genocide and torture
questions.explanation: Jus cogens are fundamental, universal legal principles that cannot be violated or suspended by any state, representing the highest legal standards.

questions.text: What does the 'responsibility to protect' (R2P) doctrine address?
options: The duty of nations to protect their borders
International community's responsibility to intervene when states fail to protect populations from mass atrocities
The obligation of states to protect foreign investments
questions.explanation: R2P establishes that states have a responsibility to protect their citizens from genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity, with the international community able to intervene when states fail.

questions.text: What does 'stateless nation' describe?
options: An ethnic or cultural group with identity and territory but without its own sovereign state
questions.explanation: Stateless nations are cultural or ethnic groups that possess a distinct identity and historical territory but lack sovereign statehood, such as the Kurds or Palestinians.

questions.text: What does 'secession' involve in constitutional law?
options: The formal process of amending a constitution
Withdrawal of a region from a sovereign state to establish independent statehood
The appointment of new government officials
The unification of two or more states
questions.explanation: Secession occurs when a part of an existing state formally withdraws to become an independent sovereign entity, often subject to constitutional and legal debates.

questions.text: What does the 'self-determination' principle allow?
options: Peoples to freely determine their political status and pursue their development
The domination of one group over another
questions.explanation: Self-determination is the right of peoples to choose their own political systems and pursue development without external interference.

questions.text: What is the 'good offices' role in international diplomacy?
options: A neutral third party facilitating communication and negotiation between disputing parties
questions.explanation: Good offices are when a third party provides a neutral forum or channels of communication to help disputing parties negotiate without directly intervening in substantive matters.

questions.text: What does 'summit diplomacy' practice involve?
options: Direct meetings and negotiations between heads of state or government
Multilateral conferences at the ministerial level
questions.explanation: Summit diplomacy occurs when heads of state or government meet directly, often to resolve major issues or establish broad policy frameworks.

questions.text: What does 'track II diplomacy' concept involve?
options: Unofficial, non-governmental interactions between conflict parties to build trust and explore solutions
questions.explanation: Track II diplomacy involves unofficial dialogues between non-governmental actors to build understanding and explore alternatives, complementing official diplomatic channels.

questions.text: What does 'dual mandate' principle refer to in governance?
options: Requirement for all laws to be passed twice
An official holding two distinct offices or responsibilities simultaneously
The division of legislative authority between houses
questions.explanation: A dual mandate occurs when an individual simultaneously holds two separate official positions, potentially creating conflicts of interest or competing responsibilities.

questions.text: What does 'balance of power' concept aim to achieve in international relations?
options: Prevent any single state from becoming too powerful by maintaining approximate equality among major powers
questions.explanation: Balance of power theory holds that peace and stability are maintained when power is distributed among major states to prevent any single nation from achieving hegemony.

questions.text: What does the 'security dilemma' concept describe?
options: All threats can be eliminated through arms control
States' security efforts making others feel less secure, escalating tensions
questions.explanation: The security dilemma arises when one state's defensive measures are perceived as threatening by others, leading to an escalatory spiral of military buildup.

questions.text: What does 'liberal internationalism' foreign policy approach emphasize?
options: International cooperation, multilateral institutions, and promotion of democracy and human rights
questions.explanation: Liberal internationalism promotes active engagement in international institutions, free trade, and advancing democratic values as means to achieve peace.

questions.text: What does the 'realism' school of international relations emphasize?
options: The primacy of national interest, power politics, and security in a competitive international system
The importance of international law and institutions
Human rights as the basis of foreign policy
questions.explanation: Realism views international politics as a struggle for power among self-interested states in an anarchic system, prioritizing security and national interest.

questions.text: What does the 'constructivist' approach examine in international relations?
options: How ideas, identities, and norms shape state interests and behavior
The biological basis of human behavior
questions.explanation: Constructivism emphasizes how social constructions—shared identities, norms, and beliefs—shape state interests and the international system.

questions.text: What does the 'rational actor model' assume in foreign policy analysis?
options: States make decisions through strategic calculation of costs and benefits to achieve clearly defined objectives
All decisions are based solely on public opinion
questions.explanation: The rational actor model treats states as unitary actors making decisions through systematic calculation of costs and benefits to maximize interests.

questions.text: What does the 'bureaucratic politics' model emphasize in foreign policy analysis?
options: The government as a unitary actor
How different government agencies and officials with competing interests shape foreign policy decisions
The exclusive role of the executive in foreign policy
The influence of public opinion on decisions
questions.explanation: Bureaucratic politics recognizes that foreign policy emerges from bargaining among multiple actors with different institutional interests and perspectives.

questions.text: What does the 'nexus' between domestic politics and international relations refer to?
options: The complete separation of internal and external affairs
The interactive relationship and mutual influence between domestic political processes and a state's international behavior
The dominance of international institutions over domestic affairs
The irrelevance of domestic factors to foreign policy
questions.explanation: The domestic-international nexus recognizes that domestic political dynamics influence international behavior, and international factors shape domestic politics.

questions.text: What does 'democratic peace theory' posit about international conflict?
options: Democracies are as likely to fight each other as non-democracies
Democracies rarely or never fight wars against other democracies
Democracies are more aggressive than autocracies
questions.explanation: Democratic peace theory suggests that established democracies tend not to engage in armed conflict with one another, based on shared norms and accountability mechanisms.

questions.text: What does 'economic interdependence' concept suggest about international relations?
options: All states should be economically self-sufficient
States with strong economic ties are less likely to engage in conflict
Economic relationships have no impact on political relations
Trade always leads to political rivalry
questions.explanation: Economic interdependence theory holds that mutually beneficial trade relationships create incentives for states to avoid conflict that would disrupt these benefits.

questions.text: What does the 'globalization' process involve?
options: The complete isolation of national economies
Increasing interconnectedness of economies, cultures, and political systems across the world
The elimination of all national borders
questions.explanation: Globalization encompasses the intensification of economic, cultural, political, and technological interdependence across national boundaries.

questions.text: What does 'regional integration' process involve?
options: States in a region cooperating to increase economic, political, and social integration
The break-up of existing regional arrangements
questions.explanation: Regional integration involves neighboring states establishing formal arrangements to increase cooperation and reduce barriers across the region.

questions.text: What does 'multilateralism' principle involve in international relations?
options: Coordination of policies among three or more states through common institutions or rules
questions.explanation: Multilateralism involves states working together through institutions and agreements that establish shared norms and rules for cooperation.

questions.text: What does 'international regime' concept refer to?
options: Sets of principles, norms, rules, and decision-making procedures around which expectations converge on specific issues
questions.explanation: International regimes are the formal and informal frameworks of cooperation that structure international interactions on specific policy issues.

questions.text: What does the treaty law principle 'pacta sunt servanda' mean?
options: Treaties can be ignored at any time
Treaties must be observed in good faith by the parties
Treaties require unanimous consent to be valid
questions.explanation: Pacta sunt servanda (agreements must be kept) is a fundamental principle of international law requiring states to honor treaty obligations in good faith.

questions.text: What is a 'reservation' in treaty law?
options: Excluding or modifying specific treaty provisions while accepting the rest
questions.explanation: Reservations allow states to accept a treaty while declaring specific provisions as inapplicable, often subject to acceptance by other parties.

questions.text: What does 'succession of states' address in international law?
options: The transfer of power within a single state
The replacement of one state by another in international legal obligations
questions.explanation: State succession concerns how international rights and obligations are transferred when one state is replaced by another.

questions.text: The principle of 'fiscal federalism' in Nigeria's revenue allocation system primarily addresses which challenge?
options: The complete centralization of all government revenues
The equitable distribution of revenue sources and expenditure responsibilities among federal, state, and local governments
The elimination of all state and local government taxation powers
The privatization of all public services and utilities
questions.explanation: Fiscal federalism examines how revenues are raised and expenditures are allocated across federal, state, and local governments, ensuring resources are distributed equitably among federating units.

questions.text: The 'doctrine of covering the field' in constitutional interpretation applies when federal and state laws conflict on concurrent legislative matters. What does this doctrine establish?
options: That state laws always prevail over federal laws
That federal laws prevail over state laws on concurrent matters once the federal government has legislated on the subject
That both federal and state laws operate simultaneously without any hierarchy
That the judiciary must always defer to state legislatures on all matters
questions.explanation: The doctrine of covering the field establishes that once the federal government legislates on a concurrent legislative subject, federal law takes precedence and effectively displaces any inconsistent state legislation.

questions.text: The 'principle of proportionality' in constitutional adjudication requires that government actions limiting fundamental rights must satisfy which condition?
options: The action must achieve any government objective without justification
The action must be proportionate to the legitimate objective pursued and not excessively restrict rights
The action must always be approved by the legislature before implementation
The action must completely eliminate all rights in all circumstances
questions.explanation: Proportionality requires that government restrictions on fundamental rights must be rationally connected to a legitimate purpose, be minimally impairing of the right, and proportionately balance individual rights against societal interests.

questions.text: The 'dialogue theory' in constitutional interpretation between courts and legislatures suggests that
options: Courts should never strike down any legislation passed by parliament
Courts and legislatures engage in ongoing exchange where judicial decisions can prompt legislative responses and reforms
Only the legislature has authority to interpret constitutional provisions
Courts must always defer to executive interpretations of the constitution
questions.explanation: Dialogue theory posits that constitutional interpretation is an ongoing conversation between courts and legislatures, where judicial invalidation of laws can trigger legislative reconsideration and reform, fostering democratic deliberation.
